definition: Artificial imagination is a narrow subcomponent of artificial general intelligence which generates, simulates, and facilitates real or possible fiction models to create predictions, inventions, or conscious experiences.
details: The term artificial imagination is also used to describe a property of machines or programs. Some of the traits that researchers hope to simulate include creativity, vision, digital art, humor, and satire. Research topics include how to model visual or auditory imagination and how to model or filter content based on human emotions. Some articles on the topic speculate on how artificial imagination may evolve to create an artificial world "people may be comfortable enough to escape from the real world". Some researchers such as G. Schleis and M. Rizki have focused on using artificial neural networks to simulate artificial imagination. Another important project is being led by Hiroharu Kato and Tatsuya Harada at the University of Tokyo in Japan. They have developed a computer capable of translating a description of an object into an image, which could be the easiest way to define what imagination is. Their idea is based on the concept of an image as a series of pixels divided into short sequences that correspond to a specific part of an image. explainer.lead: Artificial imagination is the attempt to make machines generate or simulate possible scenarios, images, inventions, or experiences rather than only process what is directly given. It matters because such abilities could support prediction and creativity, while also raising questions about artificial worlds and conscious experience.

tiers.eli5: Imagine describing a made-up animal and having a computer picture it, even though it has never seen that exact animal. Artificial imagination is about giving computers that kind of ability to picture possibilities, tell stories, or invent things. Researchers are still working out how to model these abilities.
tiers.practitioner: Work in this area includes neural-network simulations of imagination, text-to-image generation, and modelling or filtering content according to human emotions. A practical system must turn an input such as an object description into a plausible output, but plausibility alone does not establish creativity, consciousness, or general intelligence.
tiers.paperLevel: Artificial imagination is defined as a narrow subcomponent of artificial general intelligence that generates, simulates, and facilitates real or possible fiction models for predictions, inventions, or conscious experiences. G. Schleis and M. Rizki have explored neural-network simulations, while Hiroharu Kato and Tatsuya Harada have studied description-to-image generation using visual words and statistical distributions. Major open problems include modelling visual and auditory imagination and representing emotionally relevant content.

explainer.example: Hiroharu Kato and Tatsuya Harada's University of Tokyo project takes a description of an object and produces an image of it. Their approach treats an image as pixel sequences called visual words and uses statistical distributions to interpret them.

explainer.intuition: Human imagination lets us consider things that are absent, hypothetical, or new. Artificial imagination aims to reproduce parts of that ability computationally, without implying that a machine has the full richness of human experience.
howItWorks: Start with an input or goal, such as a written description of an object.
Represent useful pieces of the problem, for example dividing an image into short pixel sequences called visual words.
Use a model, such as an artificial neural network or statistical distribution, to relate those pieces to the input.
Generate an output such as an image, prediction, or possible invention, then assess whether it fits the intended task.
explainer.whyItMatters: It connects machine creativity with prediction, invention, digital art, and possible simulated experiences. It also provides a focused way to study particular imaginative abilities without claiming to have built artificial general intelligence.
misconceptions: It is not another name for artificial general intelligence; it is described as a narrow subcomponent of that broader goal.
Generating a convincing image or story does not by itself show that a machine has conscious experiences.
It is broader than image generation: proposed traits also include vision, humor, satire, and creativity.
